opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the hardest problems in our field, and people outside often underestimate it. When you look at a popular open-source project, you see the GitHub stars and the download numbers, and it looks like a huge success. But behind that there's often a very small group of people doing an enormous amount of unglamorous work: reviewing pull requests, fixing bugs reported by users who run on hardware you've never seen, keeping up with new models that come out every week, and making sure nothing breaks for the thousands of people who depend on you.

For infrastructure specifically, like inference engines, the problem is even sharper. An application-level project can sometimes be "done." Infrastructure is never done. The hardware changes, the model architectures change, the frameworks underneath you change. If you stop maintaining it for three months, it's basically dead, because the ecosystem moves so fast. So you need sustained effort, and sustained effort needs sustained resources: people, GPUs, CI machines. Testing on real GPUs is expensive. That's not something a few students can pay for out of pocket.

In the academic setting, the incentives don't really line up either. As a PhD student, what you're rewarded for is papers. Maintaining a codebase, answering issues at midnight, refactoring so other people can contribute more easily, none of that counts as a publication. So there's a real tension between what's good for the community and what's good for your career, at least in the traditional evaluation system.

What I've seen work is a kind of middle path. The project stays neutral and community-driven, but many companies contribute, because they all benefit from a shared foundation rather than each building their own. Hardware vendors want their chips supported, model companies want their models to run well on day one, cloud providers want a reliable engine. If you can make the project a place where all of them feel they have a stake, and no single one of them controls it, then you get resources without losing the open nature. Foundations and neutral governance help with that.

But it requires a lot of trust-building and a lot of what I'd call community work, not just technical work. You have to think carefully about code architecture so that contributors from different companies can work in parallel without stepping on each other. You have to be honest about what you'll accept and what you won't. And honestly, you need a few people who just care deeply about the project and are willing to carry it through the hard periods. In the end, open source is sustained by people, and the question is how to make it possible for those people to keep doing it without burning out.

r001.rationale: It says popular projects may rely on “a very small group of people” doing extensive maintenance while thousands depend on them.

r002.rationale: It explains that infrastructure needs sustained resources, but does not say investment tends to arrive only after problems emerge.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's one of the hardest problems in this field, and I say that as someone who has lived it from the inside with vLLM.

The first thing people don't realize is that the hard part isn't writing the code. The hard part is everything that happens after the code exists. Once a project becomes infrastructure, meaning other people's products depend on it, you inherit an obligation you never signed up for. Every issue is urgent to the person filing it. Every model release means someone expects support within days. Every hardware vendor wants their chip to be first-class. And none of that comes with a budget attached.

Without a company, you basically have three sources of labor. Students, who are motivated but graduate. Volunteers, who are motivated but have day jobs. And engineers from companies that use the project, who are great, but their priorities follow their employer's priorities. So a feature gets built when it matters to someone's product, and then the person who built it gets reassigned and nobody maintains it. I've seen so many pull requests that were technically excellent and then became orphans six months later.

The second difficulty is that maintenance is invisible work. Reviewing a PR carefully, writing a design document, refusing a feature because it will make the architecture worse, keeping CI green across ten hardware backends, none of that produces a paper or a demo. In academia you don't get credit for it. In industry you get credit for it only if your manager understands open source, and many don't. So the incentives push everyone toward adding things and nobody toward holding the thing together.

What I think actually works is a few things. One is having a small core group that treats the project as their primary identity, not a side project. For vLLM that meant people who genuinely decided, this is what I do. Two is being very honest with corporate contributors about what the deal is. You can land your feature, but you also own it, and if you disappear we will remove it. Three is some neutral money. It doesn't need to be a company, but somebody has to pay for the CI machines and for at least a couple of people to do the boring work full time. Foundations help with the legal side, but foundations don't write code.

And I'll say the uncomfortable part. Most projects at this scale eventually either get a company behind them or they decay. I don't think that's a moral failure, it's just gravity. The question is whether you can build the governance early enough that when the company shows up, the project stays the community's project rather than becoming a product with an open-source license attached. That's the balance we think about constantly.

r001.rationale: It describes projects that other products depend on and says sustaining them requires a small core group, while other contributors may leave their work unmaintained.

r002.rationale: It says infrastructure work lacks a budget and needs neutral funding, but does not claim investment tends to arrive only after problems emerge.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s very difficult, because building something useful and sustaining it are quite different problems. One person can have a good idea and write the initial implementation. But once people depend on it, you have issues to investigate, releases to maintain, compatibility problems, and questions to answer. That work continues even when the maintainer’s interests or circumstances change.

Without a company behind it, that responsibility can fall on a few people doing it in their spare time. Having lots of users doesn’t necessarily mean you have enough maintainers, or funding to support them.

So I think the important question is how you turn users into people who share responsibility for the project. Can companies that depend on it contribute engineering time or funding? Can new contributors gradually take ownership? A company can provide continuity, but even without one, you need some structure that lets the project survive beyond any individual’s availability.

r001.rationale: It says that without a company, responsibility can fall on a few people doing the work in their spare time, even when many users depend on the project.

r002.rationale: It discusses the difficulty of sustaining infrastructure and possible ways to support it, but does not say investment tends to happen only after problems emerge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s very difficult, because building something useful and maintaining it over time are two different problems. You might start a project because you’re excited about a technical idea, but once people depend on it, you have bug reports, compatibility issues, documentation, and requests for support. That work keeps coming even when your own interests move on.

Without a company behind it, the challenge is finding people who have both the motivation and the time to take responsibility. A lot of users doesn’t automatically mean a lot of maintainers. So I think you need to make it easy for contributors to become owners of parts of the project, and ideally find support from organizations that depend on it. Otherwise, you’re relying on a few people’s spare time, and that’s a fragile foundation for infrastructure.

r001.rationale: It says users do not automatically become maintainers and that without organizational support the project relies on a few people’s spare time.

r002.rationale: It discusses the difficulty of securing support and says organizations that depend on a project may help, but does not say investment tends to happen only after problems emerge.
